title: Black Holes: Event Horizons, Singularities, and Spacetime Curvature
executive_summary: A black hole is a region of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing — not even light or electromagnetic radiation — can escape from it. The theory of general relativity predicts that a sufficiently compact mass can deform spacetime to form a black hole.
image_caption: Supermassive black hole accretion disk rendering.

key_sections.title: The Event Horizon and Schwarzschild Radius
key_sections.content: The event horizon is the boundary surrounding a black hole beyond which no matter or radiation can escape. Its radius is called the Schwarzschild radius (r_s = 2GM/c^2). For a stellar-mass black hole of 10 solar masses, r_s is approximately 30 km.

key_sections.title: Stellar vs. Supermassive Black Holes
key_sections.content: Stellar black holes form when massive stars (>20 solar masses) collapse at the end of their lifecycle. Supermassive black holes (millions to billions of solar masses) reside at the centers of almost all galaxies, including Sagittarius A* at the center of the Milky Way.

key_sections.title: Hawking Radiation and Black Hole Evaporation
key_sections.content: Theoretical physicist Stephen Hawking demonstrated that quantum vacuum fluctuations near the event horizon allow black holes to emit faint thermal radiation (Hawking radiation), causing them to slowly lose mass and eventually evaporate over cosmic timescales.
